Simmi est arrivée à l’aube de l’âge adul: Simmi arrived in Canada on the cusp of adulthood. It was in Montréal that she, her mother and her sister set down their bags and filed a refugee claim in a country that had been presented to them as open and welcoming. The people, at least, were welcoming. It is the openness of bureaucrats they are running up against today.
Pour éviter la déportation vers l’Inde,: To avoid deportation to India, Harpreet Kaur and her mother, Paramjit Kaur, have been reduced to trying their last chance: they have decided to file a humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) application. In immigration jargon, it is the last step available to them, after the rejection of their refugee claim, to try to regularize their status.
Regard sur le parcours que suivent en si: A look at the path that many asylum seekers in Canada follow in silence.
<strong>Le chemin qui mène à une demande: The road to a humanitarian and compassionate application
Les personnes qui ne sont pas admissible: People who are not eligible to become permanent residents and who cannot be classified in other categories can apply to stay in Canada permanently on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.
Plusieurs facteurs peuvent être pris en: Several factors may be taken into consideration when assessing a humanitarian and compassionate application, for example:
Liens tissés avec la communauté au Canad: Ties established with the community in Canada
Intérêt supérieur d’un enfant: The best interests of a child
Raisons liées à l’état de santé du deman: Reasons related to the applicant's health
Facteurs dans le pays d’origine non liés: Factors in the country of origin not related to the protection claim
Simmi Sunshine – le nom sous lequel on c: Simmi Sunshine – the name by which Harpreet is known in the yoga and personal development community – and her mother, both originally from Punjab, a state in northern India, could be deported and forced to leave Montréal at any moment.
« Ça fait 14 ans que je garde cette lutt: “For 14 years, I've been keeping this struggle in the dark. It's a battle, and we've fought it alone, my mother, my sister and I,” Simmi explains. “I only shared our immigration situation with a few people because I felt a lot of shame and thought people would judge us.”
« Pour moi, la priorité quand je suis ar: “For me, the priority when I arrived in Canada was to learn French. So I spent four years learning it. Not because I was forced to, but because I told myself I wanted to be part of this society,” she says.
En dernier recours, elles ont entamé des: As a last resort, they began the process of filing a humanitarian and compassionate application. It was rejected in the first days of the pandemic. Simmi and her lawyer now have to appeal the rejection of that application.
Simmi, du haut de ses 32 ans, ne connaît: At 32, Simmi doesn't really know Punjab, which she left as a child. She has lived in Montréal for 14 years and built her life here.
Le 25 novembre dernier, Simmi tente le t: On November 25, Simmi decided to go all in and launched a crowdfunding campaign on <l1>the GoFundMe platform</l1>. It was this public cry from the heart that led to our meeting.
<strong>« </strong>Quelques milliers de: “A few thousand dollars can make the difference, but not having them is terrifying. You tell yourself, ‘Here I am in this situation that could change my whole life.’ I know what anxiety is. I know what fear is. They make you feel so small. You understand that what's happening is reality,” she says. A reality that could flip overnight, and for the worse.
Simmi a décidé de solliciter les dons du: Simmi decided to ask the public for donations and to seek help from her social circles because she believes she and her mother have not always been well represented.
Quelques jours après notre première renc: A few days after our first meeting, we see Simmi again at a Christmas market organized by her and some friends. It's a bazaar in the restaurant O.Noir, where several tables are lined up with jewellery and teas or natural soaps. A DJ is focused behind his sound table, playing music that evokes the atmosphere of certain electronic music festivals.
À quelques semaines du temps des fêtes,: A few weeks before the holidays, Simmi took part in a bazaar. She was selling clothes she no longer wears, in keeping with the spirit of this Christmas market organized with friends to “reduce overconsumption.” Photo: Anaïs Elboujdaïni
Simmi vend des vêtements de seconde main: Simmi sells secondhand clothes and chats with several people who now know about her situation. She didn't sleep the night before and is worried about the proceedings, which are following their course.
Sa voisine d’étal est une amie : Laurenc: Her neighbour at the next stall is a friend: Laurence Boisseau. A psychology graduate, she is now a coach. She and Simmi met at a yoga workshop.
« J’avais entendu entre les branches que: “I had heard through the grapevine that her situation was complicated, but I never could have guessed this was what she was going through,” she says, as we sit on a mat in her corner of the market. “She's an inspiring, strong person [...] You always feel welcomed by her, and you feel safe going to her.”
« Je ne savais pas du tout ce qu’elle tr: “I had no idea what she was going through,” Laurence repeats, speaking about Simmi's immigration situation. She found out when, to her great surprise, she saw the GoFundMe crowdfunding campaign. “I was proud of her for telling her story,” says the young woman. I ask her what Montréal would lose if Simmi and her mother were deported: “I think Simmi has a lot of friends here. She brings so much to the people around her, so it would definitely be a big loss to tear her away from her family. She's been cultivating a network for 14 years, and someone dear to us would be taken away. I find that really sad [...] You get the feeling it's just bureaucratic, as a situation.”
Cette situation est loin d’être isolée,: This situation is far from isolated, says M<sup>e</sup> Mylène Barrière, a lawyer with the Clinique pour la justice migrante. For several years, this immigration law specialist has observed a deterioration in access to justice.
« On voit des gens qui sont dans une sit: “We see people in precarious situations and they're asked for high fees. Some will manage, they'll borrow from here and there, but it makes them enormously more precarious,” says M<sup>e</sup> Barrière.
Un rapport des chercheurs Craig Damian S: A report by researchers Craig Damian Smith, Sean Rehaag and Trevor Farrow of York University estimates that the quality of representation is one of the biggest factors affecting the outcome of a refugee claim: “It is a significant and long-standing problem in terms of its impact on efficiency, outcomes and access to justice,” the report states.
Une conclusion qui peut être étendue au: A conclusion that can be extended to the world of humanitarian and compassionate applications, Simmi believes.
« Nous avons embauché quelqu’un en qui n: “We hired someone we thought we could trust to speak on our behalf. I feel that the way this lawyer presented our case, and represented us, was, let's say, sloppy. It had an incredibly negative impact. That's why having a lawyer who knows the system, who knows how to present your situation so that it can actually be heard by the judge, is essential,” says Simmi, who did not have enough funds at the time to pay for a lawyer.
« Si vous avez un avocat, ou simplement: “If you have a lawyer, or simply someone who acts a bit like a lawyer but doesn't know what they're doing, it puts you in a situation like mine, where you find yourself in a 14-year battle to prove that yes, this really is my story. Our story clearly wasn't presented properly. Now, my intention is to have the support I need to be able to present my case.”
Pour des raisons de sécurité, la famille: For safety reasons, Simmi's family has to flee India.
« Nous avons d’abord immigré aux États-U: “We first immigrated to the United States, my father, my mother and my sister. Then we claimed asylum in Canada, so that complicated our case.” It should be noted that the refugee claim was filed after she saw her father deported to India.
« Mon père a été détenu pendant un an av: “My father was detained for a year before being deported. At that point, it was extremely frightening for us, three women on our own. We were advised by people around us, who told us to claim asylum in Canada.”
En raison de leur statut irrégulier, Sim: Because of their irregular status, Simmi and her mother have been unable to leave Canada for 14 years, first waiting on their refugee status, then on their humanitarian application. So many years in which they were, in a way, stuck in Canada. Unable to see her father, in one case, or her husband, in the other.
Que ce soit le mariage de sa sœur ou une: Whether it was her sister's wedding or a boat outing on the St. Lawrence River, Simmi and her mother have spent the past fourteen years in Canada, since their status does not allow them to leave the country. Photo: Anaïs Elboujdaïni
En 2023, près de 56 % des demandes pour: In 2023, nearly 56% of humanitarian and compassionate applications were rejected across the country, according to the most recent figures sent to La Converse by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC). And in 2021, 70% of humanitarian and compassionate applications received a negative response.
À l’époque, des organismes comme Cliniqu: At the time, organizations such as the Clinique pour la justice migrante denounced the situation, pointing out that before 2020, the acceptance rate for such applications was 64%.
Plus récemment, le même organisme notait: More recently, the same organization noted an increase in deportations. They nearly doubled in the first part of 2023 compared with previous years. On average, 39 people a day were deported this year, compared with 21 and 23 in the last two years.
Simmi a déposé plus de 30 lettres de sou: Simmi submitted more than 30 letters of support with her file on December 13. They are essential elements in a humanitarian and compassionate application, because integration into the community is a factor taken into account by the immigration officer who decides whether to accept or reject the application.
Un demandeur d’asile peut faire une dema: A refugee claimant can file a humanitarian and compassionate application when asylum is not granted by a member of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB).
« Ça peut être tellement aléatoire, ce q: “The decision you might get [on the refugee claim] can be so random. [...] There are a lot of decisions that could, at times, have been positive,” says M<sup>e</sup> Barrière.
Tournons, l’espace de quelques instants,: Let's turn our gaze to the past for a few moments. It is 2012, the Maple Spring is in full swing in Quebec and Barack Obama is re-elected president of the United States. 2012 is also the year Stephen Harper's Conservative government passed a series of immigration reforms.
Les conséquences de la Loi visant à prot: The consequences of the Protecting Canada's Immigration System Act are still being felt more than 10 years later.
« Avant 2012, lorsqu’ils avaient soumis: “Before 2012, when people had submitted their refugee claim, they could also submit a humanitarian application in parallel.” Why? “Because many people don't fit those criteria [for a refugee claim], which are extremely restrictive,” says M<sup>e</sup> Barrière.
« C’était beaucoup plus flexible, tout c: “It was much more flexible, everything you could put forward, and there were often very well-founded applications,” she says. “But since 2012, you just have to fight to get a decision on a humanitarian application before removal goes ahead.”
Une situation que connaît trop bien Simm: A situation Simmi knows all too well.
« Tout le processus émotionnel, d’aller: “The whole emotional process of going back and forth to court and having your case constantly refused is very hard. We've been on the deportation list for three years. So, basically, having filed a humanitarian application doesn't necessarily guarantee that we'll be granted the right to stay here. Even while we wait to see whether our humanitarian application is accepted, the government still has the right to expel us,” Simmi explains, despair in her voice.
Rencontré dans les locaux du Centre des: Met at the offices of the Immigrant Workers Centre (IWC), an organization that defends the rights of migrants, Mostafa Henaway adds: “It's a structural problem!”
Selon lui, « il faut que les agents pren: According to him, “officers have to take the whole situation into account, how the person has integrated into Quebec, the risks they face if they are sent back.” But during all that waiting time, “how do you expect people to fully integrate when they know an application doesn't cancel the risk of deportation?”
Il déplore aussi une situation que lui e: He also decries a situation that he and his IWC colleagues have been observing for some time, namely the deportation of migrants of Indian origin: “What officers tell them is that it seems to be safe to be relocated to certain parts of India, but not others. Unfortunately, if you come from one of those regions that aren't safe, you'll be doubly uprooted because you're being relocated to a place you don't know. It's like telling someone from Quebec to go take refuge in British Columbia.”
Alors que les relations diplomatiques de: With diplomatic relations between Canada and India remaining tense, notably after the killing on Canadian soil of a Sikh separatist activist from the state of Punjab, the spectre of deportation to that country can be cause for concern.
<strong>Apprendre à faire de soi son che: Learning to make a home of oneself
Le risque de la déportation et de soumet: The risk of deportation, and of submitting the wrong documents, seems to haunt Simmi and cause her great psychological distress.
« J’ai eu le privilège et l’honneur de s: “I've had the privilege and the honour of serving and supporting many people, whether in my yoga class or my dance classes. What people often tell me is that every time they're in my presence, they feel at home. And I realized that for most of my life, I felt like I didn't have a home, that my home was going to be taken from me at any moment. And so, over the years, I learned to build a home inside myself, a home that no one can take away from me, a home that will always be there,” she says, tears running down her cheeks.
Les émotions remontent : « J’ai essayé d: The emotions rise: “I've tried to build a home over the last 14 years, laying one brick at a time, alone with my mother. And over the last seven days, where I opened up to simply receive support, I feel like I'm watching my whole community come to help me lay bricks and build this home.”
